title: The periodic table
learningObjective: Understand how elements are arranged in the Periodic Table: in order of atomic number; in groups and periods; Identify an element as a metal or a non-metal according to its position in the Periodic Table; Understand how to deduce the electronic configurations of the first 20 elements from their positions in the Periodic Table; Understand how to use electrical conductivity and the acid-base character of oxides to classify elements as metals or non-metals; Understand how the electronic configuration of a main group element is related to its position in the Periodic Table; Understand why elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have similar chemical properties; Understand why the noble gases (Group 0) do not readily react

sections.title: The periodic table — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Open with a claim worth pausing on: the
**[[periodic-table]]** shows *all the elements in the universe* and is one
of the most important tools a chemist has. Not one of the most important
tools in chemistry — one of the most important tools, full stop. The
reason is one word, worth emphasising twice: **arrangement**. Because the
elements are laid out in a fixed, meaningful order, the table lets you
understand **trends in properties** and **make predictions** — including
predictions about elements nobody had ever seen.

The prediction power is not hypothetical. The modern Periodic Table was
first presented in **1869** by the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev**,
and his table is famous precisely because it left gaps for elements that
had not been discovered yet and correctly predicted their properties. This
chapter explores some of the features of that table: how the elements are
ordered, what the **groups** and **periods** mean, how the table lets you
count protons, neutrons and electrons, and how it answers the question
"metal or non-metal?".

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- say how the elements are arranged in the Periodic Table — **in order of
  atomic number**, in **groups** (columns) and **periods** (rows);
- deduce the **electronic configurations of the first 20 elements** from
  their positions in the table;
- classify an element as a **metal or a non-metal**, both from its
  position and from **electrical conductivity** and the **acid-base
  character of its oxides**;
- explain why elements in the **same group** have **similar chemical
  properties**, and why the **noble gases** barely react at all.

:::prior-knowledge
From Lesson u1:c03 you know the counting recipe — protons from the atomic
number, electrons = protons, neutrons = mass number − atomic number — and
you know electrons sit in **shells** (energy levels) around the nucleus.
From Lesson u1:c02 you know that the 118 elements are the building blocks
of everything. This chapter finally explains how that list of elements is
*organised* — and why the organisation is not arbitrary.
:::

:::key-point
The Periodic Table shows all the elements in the universe, arranged so
that trends in properties can be understood and predictions made. The
modern form was first presented in 1869 by Dmitri Mendeleev. This
chapter: arrangement (groups and periods), electronic configurations,
and the metal / non-metal split.
:::

:::misconception
"The Periodic Table is just a list of elements in alphabetical order, or
in the order they were discovered." No — it is neither. The table is
arranged **in order of atomic number** (the number of protons), which is
exactly why its patterns are meaningful: neighbouring elements differ by
one proton, and the columns line up elements whose atoms share the same
number of outer-shell electrons.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State how elements are arranged in the Periodic Table" wants the
arrangement, not the history: **in order of (increasing) atomic number,
in groups (columns) and periods (rows)**. Naming Mendeleev or 1869 earns
nothing on that question — save the history for "describe the
development of the Periodic Table" style questions if they ever appear.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.18 × 2 items — the two arrangement facts
(atomic-number order; groups and periods).
:::

sections.title: The Periodic Table — atomic number order, groups and periods
sections.markdown:
The search for patterns in chemistry during the 19th century resulted in
the modern Periodic Table, and the ordering rule fits in one line: the
elements are arranged **in order of atomic number** — the
number of protons in the nuclei of the atoms. That single rule is what
makes the table's patterns work, and it is the first half of spec 1.18.

The **vertical columns** are called **[[group]]s**. The first seven
groups are numbered from **1 to 7** and the final group is numbered
**0**. The **[[transition-metal]]s** (transition elements) form the middle
block, and at this level they
are *not* usually included in the numbering of the groups. Some groups
have names you must know: **Group 1 is the [[alkali-metal]]s**, **Group 7
is the [[halogen]]s**, and **Group 0 is the [[noble-gas]]es**.

The **horizontal rows** are called **[[period]]s**, and one detail
catches people out: **hydrogen and helium make up Period
1** — Period 1 has only two elements. The lanthanoids and actinoids are
usually dropped out of their proper places and written separately at the
bottom of the table. There is a good reason: if you put them where they
belong, everything has to be drawn slightly smaller to fit on the page,
which makes the table harder to read. For a larger version of the table
with atomic numbers, use the Periodic Table in your exam paper —
you will need it throughout the course.

:::did-you-know
You will sometimes see Group 0 labelled as Group 8. In more advanced
Periodic Tables the groups are numbered from 1 to 18, including the
transition metals — but at International GCSE you use 1–7 and 0.
:::

:::did-you-know
Most International GCSE tables stop at the end of the actinoid series,
even though more elements continue to be discovered. Although sometimes
called the "rare earth metals", the lanthanoids are actually not that
rare and are quite important in modern technology. Most of the actinoids
are unstable and undergo radioactive decay.
:::

:::cross-curricular
History of science: Mendeleev published the modern table in 1869 — and
its power was prediction. Because the table is ordered by a *property of
the atoms* (proton number) rather than by mass alone or by date of
discovery, gaps in the pattern pointed to undiscovered elements. The same
"pattern implies prediction" logic drives data-driven fields far beyond
chemistry, from epidemiology to astronomy.
:::

:::key-point
Groups (columns) run 1–7 then 0; periods (rows) run 1–7 with hydrogen
and helium alone in Period 1. Group 1 = alkali metals, Group 7 =
halogens, Group 0 = noble gases. Transition metals sit in the middle
block and are not part of the group numbering at this level. Everything
is ordered by atomic number.
:::

:::misconception
"Group 8 is the last group because it is the eighth column." At this
level the last group is **Group 0**, not Group 8 — the numbering runs
1–7 then 0, skipping the transition metals in the middle. (Full tables
number the groups 1–18 once the transition block is counted; that
numbering is *not* the International GCSE convention.)
:::

:::exam-hint
Two arrangement facts, two marks: **in order of (increasing) atomic
number** and **in groups and periods**. If asked to name a group, use the
number *or* the accepted name (alkali metals / halogens / noble gases) —
but do not call Group 0 "Group 8"; the mark scheme at this level says 0.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.18 × 3 items — atomic number as the ordering
rule; groups as columns / periods as rows; the named groups (1, 7, 0) and
the two-element Period 1.
:::

sections.title: The Periodic Table — counting protons, neutrons and electrons
sections.markdown:
Lesson u1:c03 built the counting recipe from the definitions of atomic
number and mass number; this section connects it to the chart itself,
because **most Periodic Tables have two numbers against each symbol**.
The reading rule: **the atomic number will always be the smaller
number**. The other number will either be the **mass number
of the most common isotope** of the element or the **relative atomic
mass** of the element — and the table you are using tells you which.

From there the recipe is the one you already know, restated in its
table-reading form:

- the number of **protons** in an atom is equal to the **atomic number**;
- the number of **electrons** in an atom is equal to the number of
  protons;
- the number of **neutrons** in an atom = **mass number − atomic number**.

So the Periodic Table is not just a directory of elements — it is the
input device for the particle-counting recipe. Read the smaller number,
you have the protons (and therefore the electrons, for a neutral atom);
take the larger number, subtract, you have the neutrons. That is the
whole method, and it works for every atom on the chart.

:::key-point
Two numbers per symbol: **smaller = atomic number = protons** (=
electrons in a neutral atom); **larger = mass number of the most common
isotope, or the relative atomic mass** — the table tells you which.
Neutrons = larger − smaller. The recipe from u1:c03, now wired to the
chart you will use in every exam.
:::

:::misconception
"The bigger number on the Periodic Table is always the mass number." Not
always — for many elements that second number is the **relative atomic
mass**, which need not be a whole number (chlorine's is 35.5, as you saw
in u1:c03). The reading rule survives either way: atomic number is the
*smaller* number, and for neutron counting you use the mass number of the
most common isotope when the table supplies Aᵣ instead.
:::

:::exam-hint
If a Periodic Table offers you two numbers, never guess which is which:
**the atomic number is always the smaller one** — the same point
§s04's chlorine walk-through makes. Pick the wrong number and
every count that follows (protons, electrons, neutrons) is wrong.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.18 × 2 items — reading the two numbers off a
Periodic Table cell; the three-line counting recipe from the smaller/larger
numbers.
:::

sections.title: Arranging the electrons — shells and electronic configuration
sections.markdown:
The electrons move around the nucleus in a series of levels called
**energy levels** or **[[shell]]s** — the two terms are
interchangeable, and this lesson uses both. Each energy level can only hold
a certain number of electrons; **lower energy levels are always filled
before higher ones**, and the lowest energy level is the one closest to
the nucleus — and each level has a **maximum** it can hold. The
arrangement of electrons in an atom is called its
**[[electronic-configuration]]** — and it is exam vocabulary.

The worked method, using **chlorine** as its example, is the
one to memorise. Look up the atomic number in the Periodic Table —
making sure you take the **smaller** of the two numbers if you have a
choice. Chlorine's atomic number is **17**, so a neutral chlorine atom
has 17 protons and therefore **17 electrons**. Now arrange the electrons
in shells, always completing an inner shell before you go to an outer
one: the first shell holds up to **2**, the second up to **8**, and the
third also up to **8**. For chlorine: 2 in the first, 8 in the second,
7 in the third — written **2, 8, 7**. When you finish, always **check
that the electrons add up to the right number** — here, 17.

To draw the arrangement, draw circles to represent the shells and put
dots or crosses on the circles for the electrons — you may choose either.
Hydrogen has 1 electron and helium has 2 in the first shell. The eight
Period 2 elements then fill the second shell the same way; the atoms from
sodium to argon fill the third shell in exactly the same way; and
**potassium and calcium start to fill the fourth shell**: 2,8,8,1 and
2,8,8,2. It does not matter
at this level whether you draw the electrons singly or in pairs.

:::worked-example
Chlorine, atomic number 17 (the smaller number on its Periodic Table
cell). Protons = 17, so electrons = 17. Fill shells in order, inner
before outer: first shell 2, second shell 8, third shell 17 − 10 = 7.
Electronic configuration **2, 8, 7**. Check: 2 + 8 + 7 = 17 ✓. Mark
lines: (1) reads the atomic number as the smaller number; (2) fills
shells 2, 8, then the remainder; (3) checks the total against 17.
:::

:::key-point
The arrangement of electrons in an atom is its **electronic
configuration**. Shells fill inner-before-outer; capacities at this level
are 2, 8, 8. Always finish with the sum check: the electrons must add up
to the atomic number.
:::

:::maths-skills
The sum check is arithmetic, and it is also a marking gift: 2 + 8 + 7 =
17 costs one line and catches the single most common slip (writing 2, 8,
8 for chlorine because "the third shell holds 8"). If the sum does not
equal the atomic number, the configuration is wrong — find which shell
took the extra electron before you write anything else.
:::

:::misconception
"The circles in the diagram are the paths the electrons travel along."
No — drawing circles does **not** imply the
electrons are orbiting the nucleus along the circles. The circles
represent **energy levels**; the further a level is from the nucleus,
the higher its energy, and it is impossible to work out exactly how an
electron moves within its level.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Shell" and "energy level" are used interchangeably, and **both terms
are accepted in the examination** — use
whichever you prefer, consistently. Two drawing conventions are also
both acceptable: helium's two electrons as a pair or on opposite sides
of the circle, and electrons drawn singly or in pairs throughout.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.19 × 3 items — the shell capacities (2, 8, 8) and
inner-before-outer filling; the chlorine 2, 8, 7 walk-through; potassium and
calcium as the fourth-shell starters.
:::

sections.title: Electronic configurations of the first 20 elements
sections.markdown:
The **electronic configurations of the first 20 elements** in the
Periodic Table lay out a pattern — hydrogen and helium filling
the first shell, lithium to neon filling the second (2,1 up to 2,8), and
sodium to argon filling the third in exactly the same pattern (2,8,1 up
to 2,8,8). The figure's caption ends with the phrase "10 more elements":
potassium and calcium, the 19th and 20th, start a new shell — 2,8,8,1 and
2,8,8,2 — because the third shell is full at 8 *at this level*.

That is the whole content of spec 1.19: given any of the first 20
elements, you can deduce its electronic configuration from its position
in the Periodic Table — atomic number from the table, then fill shells
2, 8, 8, then the fourth. The figure is worth internalising rather than
memorising: the pattern *is* the table, one electron at a time.

Two honest boundaries. First, the simple
filling pattern works only up to calcium: "working out what is in their
inner shells is much more difficult — the simple patterns we have
described don't work beyond calcium" (that is why this spec stops at 20).
Second, the real machinery (an extension insight): the third
shell can actually hold up to 18 electrons, and 2 electrons go into the
fourth shell *before* the third is complete because the 4s subshell sits
lower in energy than the 3d. You do not need subshells at this level;
you need to know that the simple 2, 8, 8 picture is the model the exam
wants for the first 20 elements.

:::key-point
First 20 elements, one pattern: shells fill 2, 8, 8, then 2 — H/He
(1st shell), Li→Ne (2nd, 2,1…2,8), Na→Ar (3rd, 2,8,1…2,8,8), K and Ca
start the fourth shell (2,8,8,1 and 2,8,8,2). The simple pattern stops
at calcium; the exam tests exactly the first 20.
:::

:::misconception
"Potassium's configuration is 2, 8, 9, 1 — the third shell holds 18, so
why not keep filling it?" At International GCSE the third shell is
treated as full at **8**: potassium is **2, 8, 8, 1** and calcium is
**2, 8, 8, 2**. (The deeper story — 4s before 3d, a third shell that can
truly hold 18 — is extension material and *not* part of the model the
mark scheme uses for the first 20 elements.)
:::

:::exam-hint
"Deduce the electronic configuration of X (Z ≤ 20)" is a two-step
answer: atomic number from the Periodic Table, then fill 2, 8, 8, then
the fourth shell — and show the commas (2, 8, 1). Write the numbers with
commas exactly; a string like "281" is ambiguous and can lose the mark.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.19 × 3 items — deduce configurations across the
first 20 (H→He, Li→Ne, Na→Ar, K, Ca); the "pattern stops at calcium"
boundary.
:::

sections.title: Two important facts — groups and outer-shell electrons
sections.markdown:
Two facts turn the Periodic Table into a shortcut for electronic
configurations, and they are worth quoting exactly:

- **Elements in the same group in the Periodic Table have the same
  number of electrons in their [[outer-shell]].**
- **The number of electrons in the outer shell is the same as the group
  number, for Groups 1 to 7.**

The shortcut in action, with three elements you will never need a diagram
for again: barium sits in **Group 2**, so it has
**2 electrons in its outer shell** — the same as every other Group 2
element; **iodine** (Group 7) has **7** outer-shell electrons;
**lead** (Group 4) has **4**. One look at the column, one answer — no
shell-filling required. (The boundary, honestly: working out what is in
the *inner* shells is much more difficult, because the simple patterns do
not work beyond calcium.)

Notice what the first fact really says: a group is a column of atoms
whose outer shells match. That is why group membership — not mass, not
density, not colour — is the deep classifier of chemical behaviour. The
next section adds the period side of the story (shells), and then the
whole "configuration ↔ position" link of spec 1.22 is in your hands.

:::worked-example
Deduce the outer-shell electrons without any shell-filling: barium —
read its column, Group 2 → **2 outer electrons**. Iodine — Group 7 →
**7 outer electrons**. Lead — Group 4 → **4 outer electrons**. Mark
lines: (1) identifies the group number; (2) states outer electrons =
group number (Groups 1–7 only); (3) does not attempt inner shells.
:::

:::key-point
Same group ⇒ same number of outer-shell electrons; and for Groups 1–7,
outer-shell electrons = group number. Group 2 means 2 outer electrons,
Group 7 means 7 — for any element in the column, however heavy.
:::

:::misconception
"Barium is in Period 6, so it has 6 outer-shell electrons." That
confuses the two axes: **period counts shells, group counts outer-shell
electrons** (Groups 1–7). Barium: Group 2 → 2 outer electrons; Period 6
→ 6 *shells* in use. The next section (§s07) pins the period side down.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the number of electrons in the outer shell of X" for any Group
1–7 element is a one-step mark: the group number. The examiner is
testing the shortcut, not a diagram — drawing the full shells for, say,
iodine wastes time and invites arithmetic slips.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.22 × 3 items — outer electrons = group number
(Groups 1–7) for barium, iodine, lead; same group ⇒ same outer count.
:::

sections.title: Period numbers, and why groups share chemical properties
sections.markdown:
The period axis gets its own rule: **the period number gives the number
of occupied shells, or the highest occupied shell**.
So calcium (electronic configuration 2, 8, 8, 2) is in **Period 4** and
has four shells occupied, with its outermost electron in the fourth
shell. Iodine is in **Period 5** — five occupied shells — and because it
is *also* in **Group 7**, you can deduce it has **7 electrons in the
fifth shell**. Group gives the outer count, period gives the shell
count: together they locate an element's chemistry exactly.

Now the deeper question — why do the columns behave like families? The
answer is the section's own heading: **elements in the same group in the
Periodic Table have similar chemical properties**. The evidence is a
trio of reaction families: *all* Group 1 elements react vigorously with
water to form hydrogen and hydroxides with similar formulae — LiOH,
NaOH, KOH; *all* Group 7 elements react with hydrogen to form compounds
with similar formulae — HF, HCl, HBr; *all* Group 2 elements form
chlorides with similar formulae — MgCl₂, CaCl₂. Similar formulas come
from similar outer-shell electron counts.

And the *reason* reactions match is the electron bookkeeping you built
in §s04: **the reactions of atoms depend on how many electrons there are
in their outer shell** — those are the electrons that get involved when
elements bond. Elements in the same group (apart from helium in Group 0)
have the same number of outer-shell electrons, **therefore they react in
similar ways**. A historical wrinkle: the
noble-gas group is called Group 0 (not Group 8) because when those gases
were first discovered they were believed to combine with nothing —
**zero combining power ([[valency]])**. It is the only group whose
number does not tell you the outer-electron count: noble gases (except
helium) have **8** outer electrons. In Chapters 7 and 8 you will see
atoms losing, gaining or sharing electrons to reach 8 — the noble gases
already have 8, so they do not bother.

:::key-point
Period number = number of occupied shells (calcium: 2, 8, 8, 2 →
Period 4). Same group ⇒ same outer-shell count ⇒ similar chemical
properties — Group 1 hydroxides LiOH/NaOH/KOH, Group 7 hydrides
HF/HCl/HBr, Group 2 chlorides MgCl₂/CaCl₂. Reactions depend on
outer-shell electrons; helium is the one Group 0 exception (2 outer
electrons).
:::

:::misconception
"Group 0 elements have 0 electrons in their outer shell — the number is
the count, like Groups 1–7." No: Group 0 is the one group where the
number is *not* the outer-electron count. The name comes from the old
idea of zero combining power (valency). Noble gases other than helium
have **8** outer-shell electrons (a full shell), which is precisely why
they were thought to have zero combining power.
:::

:::exam-hint
To deduce a configuration from position alone, use **both** axes:
iodine is Period 5 *and* Group 7, so its outer electrons are 7 *in the
fifth shell*, and the full stack is 2, 8, 8, 8, 7. "Explain why
elements in the same group have similar chemical properties" wants the
causal chain: same group → same number of outer-shell electrons →
outer electrons are the ones involved in reactions → similar reactions.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.22 × 2 items (period = occupied shells; iodine
via group + period); spec 1.23 × 2 items (the three formula-family examples;
the outer-electron causal chain).
:::

sections.title: The noble gases — full shells, no reactions
sections.markdown:
The **Group 0** elements are known as the **noble gases** because they
are almost completely unreactive — in fact the two at the top of the
group, **helium and neon, don't react with anything**. The
electron-counting picture explains the group at a glance: the elements of
Group 0 have **8 electrons in their outer shell** (apart from helium,
which has **2**) — and either way, the outer shell is **full**.

That fullness is the whole explanation, stated as the exam answer: the lack of reactivity of the noble gases is associated with
their electronic configurations — **the outer shell is full, and so there
is no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons in a chemical reaction**.
Every reaction you will meet in Chapters 7 and 8 happens because an atom
is chasing a full outer shell (losing, gaining or sharing electrons to
get there). The noble gases start with the prize; they have nothing to
chase.

An extension honesty box for the curious:
in reality the outer shells of argon, krypton, xenon and radon are *not*
full — only helium and neon have truly full outer shells, because the
third shell can hold up to 18 electrons and the fourth up to 32. That is
extension work, not exam material — but it explains why "full outer
shell" is a *model* that happens to be exactly right for the two
lightest noble gases and right-in-effect for the rest at this level.

:::key-point
Noble gases (Group 0): 8 outer-shell electrons except helium (2). They
are almost completely unreactive — helium and neon react with nothing —
because the outer shell is full: no tendency to lose, gain or share
electrons. That is the whole answer to spec 1.24.
:::

:::misconception
"Helium must have 8 outer electrons to be a noble gas." Helium has
**2** — and that is a full first shell (the first shell only holds 2),
which is why helium sits in Group 0 despite never having an octet. The
unreactivity rule is **full outer shell**, not "8 electrons" as such;
8 is just what a full outer shell looks like for every noble gas except
the first.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Why are the noble gases unreactive?" is a one-cause answer and the
cause must be electronic: **full outer shell → no tendency to lose,
gain or share electrons**. Answers based on "they are stable" or "they
are gases" earn nothing — name the electron arrangement. If the question
adds "(except helium)", show you know why: 2 electrons already fill the
first shell.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.24 × 2 items — the full-outer-shell explanation;
helium's 2 as the exception that still satisfies the rule.
:::

sections.title: Metals and non-metals in the Periodic Table
sections.markdown:
Split the Periodic Table roughly down the middle and you have the oldest
classification in chemistry: **the metals are on the left-hand side and
the non-metals are on the right-hand side** — but the honest sentence
comes straight after: *in practice there is a lot of uncertainty on the
dividing line*, and
**arsenic (As)** is the classic example of an element with properties
of both metals and non-metals. Position gives you the default answer
(spec 1.21); the two property tests of §s10 give you the deciding answer
when the position is borderline (spec 1.20).

Two footnotes, both worth knowing. First,
the **lanthanoids and actinoids** — the two detached rows at the bottom
of the table — belong to the metal side; most of the actinoids are
unstable and undergo radioactive decay, as §s02 noted. Second, the great
misfit: **hydrogen**. It has 1 electron in its outer
shell, and it sits at the top of Group 1's column on almost every chart
— but it is **not** a Group 1 element in behaviour, because it "does not
have similar properties to the other elements in Group 1: it is not a
metal and does not have similar chemical properties to the alkali
metals". Hydrogen is a non-metal that happens to be drawn on the wrong
side of the line for convenience. (The curious can search "metallic
hydrogen" — planetary-core territory, and not exam material.)

:::key-point
Metals: left-hand side. Non-metals: right-hand side. The dividing line
is genuinely fuzzy — arsenic shows properties of both — so position is
the default classification and conductivity + oxide character (§s10)
are the tests. Hydrogen has 1 outer electron but is NOT a Group 1
metal: it is a non-metal misfit on the chart.
:::

:::misconception
"Hydrogen is a metal because it is drawn at the top of Group 1." Its
*position* on the chart is there for electron-counting convenience (one
outer electron), but its *properties* are non-metallic: it is not a
shiny, conducting, malleable solid, and it shares none of the alkali
metals' chemistry. Group membership means shared outer-shell electron
count *and* shared chemistry — hydrogen has only the first.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Identify X as a metal or non-metal from its position" — answer from the
left/right split (spec 1.21), but if the element sits near the dividing
line (boron-to-astatine staircase territory, arsenic included), say that
position is not decisive and cite the tests: conductivity and oxide
character (spec 1.20). The examiner rewards knowing *both* classification
routes and when each is trustworthy.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.21 × 3 items — left/right split; hydrogen's
misfit; arsenic as the borderline case.
:::

sections.title: Metals vs non-metals — conductivity and oxide character
sections.markdown:
There are many differences between metals and non-metals, but **two
main ones classify them**: **electrical
conductivity** and **the acid-base character of their oxides**. These two
tests are spec 1.20, and they work where position alone wobbles (that
arsenic problem from §s09).

**Test one — conductivity.** Metals conduct electricity; non-metals do
not generally conduct. The *reason* waits for Chapter 9 — metals conduct
because they contain **[[delocalised-electron]]s that are free to move**
— but the observation itself is the classifier: it is why metals such as
copper are used in electrical wires.
Non-metals do not conduct because they have no free-to-move electrons or
mobile ions — **with a few exceptions, such as [[graphite]] (a form of
carbon) and silicon**.

**Test two — oxide character.** Metals generally form **[[basic-oxide]]s**: a basic oxide reacts with **acids to form salts** — copper
forms copper(II) oxide (CuO), which reacts with sulfuric acid to form
the salt copper(II) sulfate. Non-metals generally form **[[acidic-oxide]]s**: sulfur(IV) oxide (SO₂) — familiar as one of the gases
responsible for acid rain — reacts with **bases/alkalis to form salts**;
carbon dioxide, an acidic oxide, reacts with sodium hydroxide, an alkali.
The water-solubility picture completes here: a *soluble*
basic oxide dissolves to form an **alkali** (sodium oxide + water →
sodium hydroxide solution); a *soluble* acidic oxide dissolves to form an
**acidic solution** (sulfur(IV) oxide + water → sulfurous acid).

And the exceptions box: **some metals form amphoteric oxides** — e.g. **Al₂O₃**, an **[[amphoteric-oxide]]** that
reacts with acids *and* bases — and **some non-metal oxides (e.g. CO)
are neutral**. The figures close the section with two caution photographs:
mercury, a metal that is liquid at room temperature, and shiny sulfur
crystals that are unmistakably not metal.

:::key-point
The two classifiers (spec 1.20): metals **conduct** electricity and form
**basic oxides** (react with acids → salts; soluble ones give alkalis in
water). Non-metals **do not generally conduct** (exceptions: graphite,
silicon) and form **acidic oxides** (react with bases/alkalis → salts;
soluble ones give acids in water). Exceptions: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric; CO
is a neutral oxide.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Physics link: "conducts electricity" means charge carriers are free to
move — the same free-electron picture that carries current in a circuit
you would wire in physics. Copper's job in a plug or a cable is the
delocalised-electron fact of this section; Chapter 9 gives the chemistry,
but the voltmeter-and-ammeter test is pure physics.
:::

:::misconception
"Non-metals never conduct electricity." The rule is *do not generally
conduct* — the named exceptions matter and they are worth memorising:
**graphite** and **silicon**. Classify by the default AND know the named
exceptions; a classification question built on graphite is testing
exactly this.
:::

:::exam-hint
"Classify X as a metal or non-metal using electrical conductivity and
oxide character" wants *both* tests stated and *both* answers pointed the
same way: conducts + basic oxide → metal; does not conduct (usually) +
acidic oxide → non-metal. Name the exceptions if the element is graphite,
silicon, aluminium (amphoteric oxide) or carbon monoxide (neutral oxide).
:::

oxide + water outcomes (alkali vs acidic solution); the Al₂O₃ / CO

:::

sections.title: Metals — the property list
sections.markdown:
Beyond the two classifier tests, here is the fuller character reference
for metals — a property list where almost every line carries
its own exception, which is exactly why the list teaches careful
science. Metals:

- **tend to be solids** with **high melting and boiling points**, and
  with **relatively high densities** — but as with several properties in
  this list there are exceptions: **mercury is a liquid** at room
  temperature — a full portrait of an exception: high density, shiny,
  conducts electricity, forms positive ions — liquid anyway);
- **are shiny** — they have a **[[metallic-lustre]]** — when polished or
  freshly cut;
- **are [[malleable]]** (can be hammered into shape);
- **are [[ductile]]** (can be drawn into wires);
- **are good conductors of electricity and heat**;
- **form ionic compounds** (Chapter 7);
- **form positive ions** in their compounds (Chapter 7).

Notice the two forward references: the *ionic compounds* and *positive
ions* lines both point at Chapter 7 — the bonding chapter will explain
*why* metals lose electrons. And notice which two properties were
chosen as the *classifiers* back in §s10 (conductivity, oxide character):
they are the two the list cannot hedge about, which is what made them
worth promoting to spec-level tests.

:::key-point
Metals: solids with high melting/boiling points and high densities
(mercury is the liquid exception); shiny when polished or freshly cut
(metallic lustre); malleable; ductile; good conductors of electricity
AND heat; form ionic compounds and positive ions (both Chapter 7).
:::

:::misconception
"All metals are solid with high melting points." The word doing the work
is **tend** — mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature,
the official named exception. Property
lists describe the *tendency* of a class; a single named exception is
enough to break an absolute claim.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State three properties of metals" is free marks from this list — but
pick *chemical* or *physical* ones as the question asks, and never offer
a property the element in question breaks (if the question features
mercury, "solid at room temperature" is wrong twice over). Malleable =
hammered into shape; ductile = drawn into wires — keep the two words
paired to their verbs.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.20/1.21 × 2 items — the metals property list with
the mercury exception; malleable vs ductile vocabulary.
:::

sections.title: Non-metals — the property list, and the chapter close
sections.markdown:
The mirror list, again with the hedges intact. Non-metals:

- **tend to have low melting and boiling points** (there are some
  exceptions — e.g. **carbon and silicon**);
- **tend to be brittle when they are solids**;
- **don't have the same type of shine as metals** (shiny sulfur crystals
  are still not a metal);
- **don't usually conduct electricity** — carbon in the form of
  **graphite** and silicon are again the exceptions;
- **are poor conductors of heat** — with a spectacular exception:
  **diamond is the best conductor of heat of all the elements**;
- **form both ionic and covalent compounds** (Chapters 7 and 8);
- **tend to form negative ions** in ionic compounds (Chapter 7).

That closes the chapter's classification story: position gives the
default (§s09), conductivity and oxide character give the test (§s10),
and the property lists give the texture (§s11–s12). The closing skills
to self-check: naming elements from a list by group, period and class,
and drawing electron diagrams for sodium, silicon and sulfur. This
lesson's practice is wired to the question bank below.

:::summary
- The Periodic Table arranges all the elements **in order of atomic
  number**, in **groups** (columns, 1–7 then 0) and **periods** (rows;
  H and He alone in Period 1); Group 1 = alkali metals, Group 7 =
  halogens, Group 0 = noble gases; transition metals sit between and
  are not group-numbered at this level.
- Two numbers per symbol: smaller = atomic number (protons, and
  electrons in a neutral atom); neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
- Electrons fill shells inner-before-outer (2, 8, 8 at this level); the
  arrangement is the **electronic configuration** — check the sum
  against the atomic number (chlorine: 2, 8, 7).
- **Group number = outer-shell electrons** (Groups 1–7); **period
  number = occupied shells**; same group ⇒ same outer count ⇒ similar
  chemical properties (LiOH/NaOH/KOH; HF/HCl/HBr; MgCl₂/CaCl₂).
- Noble gases: full outer shell (8, or 2 for helium) ⇒ no tendency to
  lose, gain or share ⇒ almost completely unreactive.
- Metals: left side; conduct; basic oxides; shiny, malleable, ductile,
  high-density solids (mercury the liquid exception); positive ions.
  Non-metals: right side; do not generally conduct (graphite, silicon
  except); acidic oxides; low-melting, brittle; negative ions.
  Hydrogen is the misfit: 1 outer electron, non-metal anyway.
:::

:::can-you
- [ ] state the two arrangement facts (atomic-number order; groups and
      periods) and the three named groups?
- [ ] read any Periodic Table cell — which number is the atomic number,
      and what might the other one be?
- [ ] deduce the electronic configuration of any of the first 20
      elements, with the sum check (chlorine 2, 8, 7; potassium
      2, 8, 8, 1)?
- [ ] say what the group number and the period number each tell you,
      and use both to place iodine's outer electrons?
- [ ] explain why elements in the same group react similarly, with the
      formula families as evidence?
- [ ] explain why the noble gases barely react — and why helium is the
      2-electron exception that still fits?
- [ ] classify an element as metal or non-metal from its position AND
      from conductivity + oxide character, exceptions included (Al₂O₃,
      CO, graphite, silicon)?
:::

:::misconception
"Shiny means metal — sulfur crystals are shiny, so sulfur is a metal."
The counterexample is on purpose: lustre alone is not the classifier. Sulfur is brittle, does not conduct, and forms an acidic
oxide — three non-metal verdicts against one borrowed shine. Use the two
spec tests (conductivity, oxide character) over any single property.
:::

:::exam-hint
In the exam, the supplied Periodic Table is your reference card. And
for "state the property" questions, quote the hedges: *tend to*,
*generally*, *usually* — the exceptions
(mercury, graphite, diamond's heat conduction) are exactly what separates
a list from a law.
:::
